name: Monospace
summary: Every character takes the same width, as on a typewriter or a terminal. The narrow letters get serifs or wide arms and the wide letters are squeezed. It is the voice of code, data, forms and the typewritten document.

philosophy.core_thesis: When every character has the same width, columns align without a grid and each character is a unit the reader can count.
design_principles: Give every glyph the same advance width, 0.50–0.62 em; 0.60 em is the common value.
Widen the narrow letters (i, l, j, r, f, t) with long serifs or arms, so they fill their cell.
Squeeze the wide letters (m, w, M, W) and lighten their joins, so they do not look darker than the rest.
Make look-alike characters different: 0 with a slash or a dot, l with a tail, 1 with a flag and a foot, and a clear I.
Hold a large x-height, 0.70–0.80 of the cap height, for small sizes on screens.
anti_patterns: Proportional figures or kerning in a code font
An O and a 0 that look the same
Ligatures that hide the real characters from a reader who copies the code

classification.vox_atypi: No class: fixed pitch cuts across the classes
classification.din_16518: No group: typewriter faces are filed under Gruppe V or VI
classification.note: Monospace is a rule of spacing, not of form: Courier is a slab serif, IBM Plex Mono is a grotesque with slab arms, JetBrains Mono is a neo-grotesque.

anatomy.contrast: Low: the thin parts are 0.7–1.0 of the stem.
anatomy.serifs: Slab serifs on the narrow letters (i, l, j, r) in most faces; full slabs in typewriter faces such as Courier.
anatomy.terminals: Flat or round cuts; the ends of c, e and s are cut horizontal in code fonts.
anatomy.aperture: Moderate to open, so the c and e stay clear at small sizes.
anatomy.key_letters: A zero with a slash or a dot, an l with a tail, an i with long serifs, and a squeezed m and w.

metrics.x_height: The x-height is 0.70–0.80 of the cap height and about 0.50–0.55 of the em.
metrics.contrast: The side of the o is 1.0 to 1.4 times as thick as its top.
metrics.width: Every glyph has one advance width, 0.50–0.62 em; the mean advance of a to z equals it.
metrics.figures: Tabular lining figures only, with a slashed or dotted zero.

setting.text_sizes: Set code at 12–14 px on screen and 8–10 pt in print, about 0.85–0.9 of the size of the text face beside it.
setting.display_sizes: Set titles at 24–64 px for a technical or typewritten look.
setting.leading: Set the leading at 1.4–1.6 for code blocks.
setting.tracking: Set 0 em; never track or kern a monospace, or the columns break.
setting.measure: Set 80–100 characters a line for code; 60–70 for typewritten prose.
setting.case_and_features: Turn off ligatures for code that readers copy, and turn on the slashed zero if the font has it as a feature.

pairing.rule: Pair the monospace with a proportional sans of the same family or skeleton, and use the monospace only for code, data and labels.

pairs.role: sans for the interface and prose
pairs.why: Both have a large x-height and low contrast, so code and prose sit well on one line.
Fira Sans and Fira Code come from one family, so the x-heights and weights match.

reference_faces.note: Courier Prime is an open redraw of the Courier model for screenplays; the original Courier design is not protected, but its digital fonts carry vendor licences.

emotion.target_response: Precision and candour: the reader feels raw data, a machine or a typed document with nothing hidden.

avoid_when: The text is long prose for general readers.
The brief asks for elegance or warmth.

modifiers.how: Set the prose in a proportional sans with the same x-height, and keep the monospace for code only.
Use a typewriter face with full slabs, such as Courier Prime, and a slightly rough print texture.

width.note: The advance is fixed, so the width moves only a little.

x_height_ratio.note: Courier sits near 0.42; code faces such as JetBrains Mono near 0.55.

tracking.note: Tracking breaks the columns of a monospace.

sources.title: Robert Bringhurst, The Elements of Typographic Style (Hartley & Marks, 4th ed. 2012)
